description: We are Vulcano, a team from Santiago, Chile, participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. We are working on the “Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots” challenge, aiming to build a web application that combines satellite fire hotspot records into a clear burning activity calendar. We welcome people interested in software, data analysis, visualization, Earth science, UI/UX, and teamwork to create a useful tool for fire awareness and response.
summary: FireWatch is a web application designed to help users understand how fire activity changes over time. It uses active fire detections from MODIS and VIIRS, available through NASA FIRMS, to bring observations from both instruments into a historical calendar for a selected area. Because MODIS and VIIRS detect fires at different spatial resolutions, raw hotspot counts can be misleading when compared across years. FireWatch is designed to account for these differences so users can better distinguish changes in detected fire activity from changes in how it was observed. The calendar helps researchers, land managers, and emergency response teams explore seasonal patterns, spot unusual periods, and identify when closer monitoring may be useful.
details:
FireWatch is a web prototype for exploring historical fire activity from satellite observations. The interface includes a fire map, an activity calendar, a trends view, and a data sources page. These views are designed to help users examine where hotspots were detected, identify seasonal patterns, and see which instruments contributed observations.

The project addresses a challenge in comparing fire records across years. MODIS and VIIRS observe the same areas at different spatial resolutions and may detect different numbers of hotspots. A raw count can change when the mix of sensors changes, even if fire activity stays similar. FireWatch uses NASA FIRMS active fire observations as the basis for its analysis. The goal is to make comparisons across time easier to interpret by showing the source of the observations and accounting for instrument differences when building a historical activity calendar for a selected area.

The team built the frontend with SvelteKit and TypeScript and developed a Python backend with FastAPI. The prototype is intended for researchers, land managers, and response teams who want to explore historical patterns and identify periods that merit closer investigation.

Frontend source code: https://github.com/Coragg/firesystem

Backend source code: https://github.com/Coragg/firesystem-backend
